detail.abstract: This paper studies whether firms' accumulation of artificial intelligence (AI) capital shapes their participation in the market for corporate control. We combine AI-skilled employment data with a capitalization model to estimate the implied price and accumulated quantity of installed AI capital. A one-standard-deviation increase in AI capital is associated with a 2.21-percentage-point increase in the acquisition probability. The relation remains after controlling for AI-skilled employment, data-skilled hiring, organizational capital, and patent capital, whereas AI-skilled employment alone does not exhibit the same predictive relation. Cross-sectionally, the AI--acquisition relation is stronger among large firms. AI capital also predicts firms' subsequent demand for AI-skilled labor beyond existing AI employment and prior AI hiring activity. Consistent with complementarity between installed AI capabilities and additional AI expertise, AI-rich acquirers disproportionately select targets that employ AI-skilled workers, both in realized public-to-public deals and relative to matched potential targets. We further find that the positive relation between AI capital and acquisition activity is weaker when firms face higher financing costs, consistent with financing conditions affecting firms' ability to act on acquisition opportunities. The main relation is also present in instrumental-variable estimates using firms' pre-2010 exposure to AI-intensive universities. Together, the findings show that accumulated AI capabilities are associated with both greater acquisitiveness and the acquisition of complementary AI human capital, with implications for firm boundaries and the persistence of incumbent advantage.

detail.abstract: Nigerian crude production has fallen persistently short of federal targets and OPEC quotas while approximately 2,700 well strings sit shut in as of December 2024. Public discussion attributes the inventory almost entirely to security incidents, crude theft, and missing evacuation routes. This report challenges that framing and estimates the share of the shut-in inventory attributable to wax deposition in production tubing. Drawing on eleven peer-reviewed journal articles and Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission publications, the analysis reconstructs the composition of shut-in wells across terrain, operator class, and stated cause; documents the wellestablished chemistry that makes Niger Delta crude prone to paraffin deposition; and evaluates published remediation methods for cost, downtime, and durability under Nigerian conditions. The report concludes with a three-tier screening framework that identifies wax-constrained candidates from data operators already report, without requiring new field measurements to initiate first-pass identification. Recommendations directed at the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission and at producing operators include piloting the screening framework on a defined test sample, publishing disaggregated shut-in cause data by field, and prioritizing wax intervention campaigns alongside the existing evacuation-focused reactivation agenda.

detail.abstract:
The main goal of this study was to investigate debt management on the performance of a microfinance institution in the case of Micro Financial Services (Pvt) Ltd (SFS). SFS is a registered microfinance institution that grants credit to low-income earners across Zimbabwe and was established in 2009. The performance or success, growth, and going concern of a microfinance institution is centered on granting more credit and controlling the cash flows.

From 2012 to 2015, SFS granted $3 454 058 to borrowers, and $690 811 was the total interest receivable. The total amount received was $3 869 634, out of which $3 260 067 was from SSB, but $275 235 was not received, while $46 770 was written off. Bad debts written off dropped from $ 90 000 in 2011 to $6 840 in 2012. In 2013, the amount of bad debts written off increased by $3 372, $3 924 in 2014 and further increased by $1 446 in 2015. The gradual increase in bad debts written off shows that the problem of loan defaults consistently existed in the organization. Also, the total amount not recovered in 2012 was $20 960, $69 510 in 2013, $71 780 in 2014, and $112 985 in 2015 

A review of relevant and related literature was done to identify what authors and scholars say in respect of debt management policy, policy implementation, personnel capabilities, controls, challenges, and best measures. The descriptive research design was adopted in conjunction with questionnaires and interviews, which were used qualitatively and quantitatively to collect data. The data collected was presented using tables, pie charts, and bar graphs, and the mode was used as a measure of central tendency to analyse the presented data.

Conclusion and recommendations on best debt management practices were based on the analysed data collected in a bid to satisfy questions on policy implementation, controls, and challenges to enhance performance through full debt management operations.

detail.abstract: This study examines how perceived quality, perceived value, perceived price and perceived economic situation relate to purchase intention for an innovative squeeze-bottle condiment format in Pakistan. A mixed-method design combined a consumer survey with qualitative focus-group evidence. The original survey contained 250 respondents; the SPSS analysis of the focal product uses 223 valid cases. Five-point Likert-scale measures were analyzed using Pearson correlation and multiple linear regression, while a 15-participant focus group was analyzed in NVivo. Perceived value and perceived quality showed the strongest positive correlations with purchase intention (r = .680 and r = .634), followed by perceived price (r = .558) and perceived economic situation (r = .368), all p < .001. The regression model was significant, F(4, 218) = 61.54, p < .001, and explained 53.0% of the variance in purchase intention (R² = .530; adjusted R² = .522). Perceived value had the largest standardized coefficient (β = .330), followed by perceived quality (β = .291), perceived price (β = .135) and perceived economic situation (β = .126). The findings indicate that functional value and quality perceptions are central to consumer response to packaging-led innovation.

detail.abstract: Tourism performance is routinely framed in terms of visitor arrivals, yet the policy relevance of additional trips depends partly on whether visitors remain long enough to spend in the destination. This documentary case study examines the apparent divergence between domestic-trip volume and accommodation length of stay in West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), Indonesia. It triangulates provincial tourism statistical releases for May-July 2026 with peer-reviewed research on tourism governance, attractions, community participation, and local development. BPS reported 1,332,393 domestic tourism trips in May and 1,368,707 in June; July reached approximately 1.41 million. Over the same months, average guest length of stay in star-rated hotels was 1.86, 1.88, and 1.98 days, while non-star accommodation recorded 1.55, 1.59, and 1.63 days. These series measure different populations and cannot establish a direct conversion rate from trips into nights. Instead of claiming that growth caused short stays, the paper identifies a measurement and governance problem: rising trip counts coexist with stays typically below two days in observed accommodation categories. A proposed visitorvolume-to-local-value framework links trip composition, destination circulation, accommodation capture, and local expenditure. The paper outlines testable mechanisms and a monitoring agenda, including median trip duration, visitor-night measures, tourism expenditure, inter-destination itineraries, and resident economic capture. Findings are descriptive rather than causal and support a shift toward value-sensitive performance measurement.

detail.abstract: The sublevel open stoping (SLOS) boundary problem selects, from a set of pre-computed candidate stopes, a non-overlapping subset of maximum undiscounted profit that also respects the pillar spacing required by the geotechnical design. We formulate the problem as a maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) on the stope conflict graph and, equivalently, as a weighted set-packing problem in which the block-model cells are the elements and each candidate stope, enlarged by its pillar envelope, is a set of cells. We show that the linear relaxation of the pairwise conflict formulation, on which the LP-based weighted-greedy heuristic of Kako et al. (WGL) relies, is degenerate for stope layouts: on every instance tested, its optimum is the point at which every stope takes the value 1 2 , and its bound is 10 to 137 times the optimal profit. WGL therefore reduces to a static greedy rule. Replacing the pairwise constraints by one constraint per block-model cell gives a relaxation with 16 to 226 times fewer rows that lies within 0.22 % of the optimum and is integral on half of the instances. An LP-guided greedy on this relaxation (WGL-C) is proposed. The methods are benchmarked on ten instances built from a synthetic vein block model (3,493 to 20,646 candidate stopes, up to 5.2 million conflicts), against the exact integer programme, solved with an open-source solver, and a C++ implementation of the Sandanayake heuristic (DSH). The integer programme is solved to proven optimality in 4 to 812 s. WGL-C attains a mean relative error of 1.3 % (maximum 5.1 %, optimal on five instances) in 2 to 28 s, whereas WGL averages 10.7 % and DSH 9 to 26 % depending on the order in which it processes the stopes. A case study on three zones of a Mexican polymetallic underground mine, built with the mine's life-of-mine parameters, gives dense conflict graphs and layouts of 3 to 7 stopes. On these instances the clique relaxation is integral and WGL-C returns the proven optimum in 2 to 6 s, whereas WGL falls 9 to 21 % short of the optimum and DSH up to 39 %, depending on C T k and stope order.

detail.abstract: Recent studies link child labor to worse mental health, but not to the features of work that drive this relationship. We examine this question using large-scale survey data and the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), a clinically validated screen for depressive symptoms, for 110,872 children in Punjab, Pakistan. Child labor is associated with a 5.3 percentage point higher probability of reporting at least mild depressive symptoms. To address concerns about shared family circumstances and unobserved selection, we compare children within households and full siblings, and use instrumental variables. The association remains positive across these approaches. The physical demands and time requirements of work help explain why symptoms differ across types of work: the gap between paid employment and unpaid family work narrows substantially after we account for work hours and hazardous conditions. The association is largest in the poorest households and among children not living with both parents. Our findings suggest that the costs of relying on child labor extend beyond lost schooling to depressive symptoms, and point to regulating hours and hazardous conditions and to social protection for poor households.

detail.abstract:
Acyclicity of the improvement graph plays a central role in the existence and welfare properties of bilateral equilibrium in two-sided exchange. While this provides the static foundations of equilibrium, little is known about the adjustment processes that lead to such outcomes. This paper develops a dynamic theory of bilateral equilibrium. We introduce deterministic and stochastic bilateral improvement dynamics in which agents myopically adopt profitable bilateral deviations. Under acyclicity, the associated welfare potential acts as a Lyapunov function: welfare increases along every improvement path and convergence to acyclic bilateral equilibria occurs in finite time. Introducing stochastic perturbations yields a perturbed Markov process whose long-run behavior may be analyzed using resistance-based methods. Welfare-maximizing acyclic equilibria are favored under the perturbed dynamics and receive positive limiting probability as noise vanishes. These results provide dynamic foundations for bilateral equilibrium and connect existence, welfare, adjustment, and stochastic stability in bilateral exchange.

This paper builds upon/complements the author's previous work titled 'Bilateral Equilibrium in Two-Sided Exchange: Acyclicity, Existence, and Global Compatibility', available at SSRN: http://ssrn.com/abstract=7566822.

detail.abstract: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) accounts for 59% of global textile fiber production, and its synthesis relies on antimony catalysts, a suspected human carcinogen. The enzyme Candida antarctica Lipase B (CALB) catalyzes polyester synthesis without leaving a metal residue and with more mild reaction conditions. Though there is no data on using CALB for PET specifically, it is used as a proxy here for a prospective enzymatic route. Cost is frequently cited as the barrier to adoption in general, and this paper tests that claim by deriving catalyst and energy costs for both catalysts from commodity price data and reaction stoichiometry, then applying Wright's law to determine whether learning effects in the enzyme production close the gap. Findings resulted in an enzymatic cost of $931.85 per ton against $17.62 for antimony, meaning that parity is reached only under the most optimistic learning rate scenario at ~2% of global PET output. The Jacobian sensitivity matrix confirmed the parity's sensitivity to the learning rate. The Monte Carlo simulation across 10,000 draws places the probability of parity within global production at 50.4%. The threshold analysis revealed that the binding constraint is catalyst efficiency rather than production scale.

detail.abstract: Refugee governance in the Global South often exhibits a transboundary character, particularly as major countries of asylum seek to mobilize international support for their responses. As policymaking increasingly transcends borders and governance levels, analytical frameworks must adequately capture these multi-arena dynamics. Despite the increasing use of the Multiple Streams Framework (MSF) in contexts beyond the national level, few studies explicitly consider how processes unfolding across different governance arenas shape policy outcomes. We argue that applying the framework to such settings is possible, provided careful attention is paid to how streams are constructed and how dynamics beyond the focal polity may influence their coupling. We apply the MSF to the 2016 Jordan Compact, a landmark agreement that expanded Syrian refugees' access to Jordan's labor market in exchange for international concessions. The analysis centers on stream dynamics within Jordan while situating them within broader transnational processes involving key external actors, including the United Kingdom, European Union, and World Bank. The case reveals a complex pattern in which stream alignment was facilitated by interactions with external actors, underscoring the role of transnational policy entrepreneurs.

detail.abstract: Firms are delegating a growing share of marketing and business development work to autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems that identify prospects, generate personalized communications, and in some deployments initiate contact without human review. This paper examines whether that delegation produces diminishing or negative marginal returns once it extends beyond information processing into strategic judgment, relationship development, and customer engagement. Drawing on literatures in automation research, algorithm aversion and appreciation, relationship marketing, attention economics, and AImediated communication, the paper identifies three mechanisms through which automation intensity may erode commercial effectiveness: an attention-congestion externality, in which near-zero marginal communication cost induces aggregate volume that depresses response probability for all senders; an authenticity penalty, in which recipients discount communications perceived as machine-generated; and competitive convergence, in which firms using similar generative models and optimization objectives become harder to distinguish. A conceptual economic model formalizes these mechanisms and derives conditions under which the relationship between automation intensity and effectiveness is inverted-U shaped, monotone increasing, or monotone decreasing. The paper then proposes the Human Judgment Preservation Framework (HJPF), a four-layer architecture-data intelligence, decision support, human judgment, and controlled execution-with an explicit task-allocation rule based on verifiability, reversibility, authorship sensitivity, and differentiation value. Competing evidence that automation improves relevance, consistency, and access is examined in detail. The framework is presented as a set of testable hypotheses rather than validated findings. The author, a co-owner of LORIQ Technologies, LLC, discloses a commercial interest in an AI-enabled business development platform whose design is informed by the framework.

detail.abstract: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Apache Kafka (self-managed or via Amazon MSK) are the two dominant real-time ingestion choices on AWS, yet published comparisons often rely on vendor marketing rather than reproducible data. This paper compares both using only officially published or reproducible figures: throughput ceilings, latency, total cost of ownership, and portability. Kinesis imposes a hard 1 MB/s (1,000 records/sec) write ceiling per shard against Kafka's substantially higher, non-fixed per-partition throughput. Kinesis's standard consumer latency (~200ms) drops to ~70ms with enhanced fan-out, still an order of magnitude above Kafka's single-digit-millisecond median. Using a cost model from published pricing for a 10 MB/s, 24-hour-retention workload, Kinesis costs ~$125/month versus ~$713/month for an equivalent MSK cluster, driven mainly by MSK's three-broker minimum and replicated storage. Kinesis scales linearly with throughput; MSK's broker cost stays fixed. We propose a decision framework for choosing between platforms per workload, not in the abstract.

detail.abstract: This paper focuses on narrative cognition, narrative transportation, and emotional immersion. While this scope does not emphasize a deeper examination of the paradigmatic, critical, and analytical modes, they form the foundation for a central premise: Because human beings are cognitively and psychologically predisposed toward narrative cognition, storytelling is a particularly effective form of persuasion, operating through cognitive and emotional processes that differ from the critical counterarguing and analytical scrutiny that are typically associated with traditional, fact-based informational messaging. This paper synthesizes selected foundational and interdisciplinary research across cognitive psychology, communication theory, and marketing to examine how storytelling functions as a persuasion tool in marketing and advertising, emphasizing emotional response and durability, memory recall and source dissociation, and self–brand connections. Although storytelling has been widely examined as a persuasive mechanism that influences memory recall, emotional durability, and attitude change through narrative-based cognitive and emotional processes, much of this research has remained constrained by disciplinary silos, leaving the collective influence of overlapping cognitive and psychological mechanisms insufficiently integrated into a unified explanation of narrative persuasion.This paper proposes that no single cognitive or psychological process can fully explain the persuasive influence of storytelling, which instead results from the interaction of multiple overlapping mechanisms. This paper argues that storytelling persuasion functions as a cross-disciplinary, multimechanistic framework in which related mechanisms operate in tandem, thereby giving rise to the emergent effectiveness of narrative persuasion. This synthesis highlights the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to understanding narrative persuasion.

detail.abstract: Using patent transfer and licensing data from 2002 to 2014 matched with Chinese industrial firm-level data from the Annual Survey of Industrial Firms (ASIF), this study constructs a directed, weighted technology transaction network and examines how a firm's weighted degree centrality affects firm resilience employing a two-way fixed-effects model. The results show that: (1) weighted degree centrality significantly enhances firm resilience, with information flow and continuous innovation as two mediating channels; (2) the effect is stronger for technology providers than recipients, for firm-research institution transactions than firm-firm transactions, and for technology-intensive industries than capital-or labor-intensive industries; (3) reduced network fragmentation, high-speed railway construction, and digital infrastructure development positively moderate the centrality-resilience relationship. These findings, based on historical evidence from the 2002-2014 sample period, offer policy reflections on building highstandard technology factor markets, promoting the free flow of technological factors, and leveraging digital and transportation infrastructure to enhance firm resilience and economic security.

detail.abstract: China has become Africa's single most important external economic partner in trade, infrastructure finance, and construction. This article examines whether Chinese investment functions as a catalyst for the continent's industrialisation or reproduces structures of dependency. It foregrounds African scholarly voices-above all the Congolese-Canadian analyst Patrick Mbeko, whose thesis of a "strategy of chaos and lies" frames how external powers instrumentalise African elites and resources-alongside data from the Boston University Global Development Policy Center, the China Africa Research Initiative, UNCTAD, and the 2024 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation. The article argues a conditional answer: Chinese capital has demonstrably helped close Africa's infrastructure and productive-capacity gaps, yet its developmental impact remains uneven because many projects reproduce enclave extraction, debt exposure, weak local linkages, and technology dependence. The decisive variable is African agency, illustrated by the DRC's 2018 mining code and 2025-2026 cobalt and copper export bans, Ethiopia's industrial parks, Kenya's renegotiation of the SGR, and the AfCFTA's integration project. The article further argues that the dominant Western discourse framing Chinese engagement as uniquely predatory-through charges of "debttrap diplomacy," "poor-quality" exports, and "spying"-is empirically weak and strategically motivated: the debt-trap thesis has been debunked by scholarly research, China is the world's factory to which Western multinationals themselves source production, and the most extensive global surveillance apparatus is American, not Chinese. On balance, Chinese investment is beneficial to African industrialisation, and Africa has more to gain from engagement with China than from heeding Western calls to foreclose it.

detail.abstract:
You can see the future first in San Francisco, wrote Leopold Aschenbrenner, and he was right about computation. But the future of civilization, of its energy, its population, and the way its wealth is shared, is visible first from the United Arab Emirates, where I live. From here, economic stagnation, collapsing birth rates, and wealth that no longer reaches households all look like symptoms of a single structural constraint, the stalling of a society's capacity to conceive and build on a large scale.

The constraint has three components, namely (i) the absence of effective energy abundance, (ii) a shortfall in labor input where automation has lagged, and (iii) the absence of institutions that draw in capital and talent. Since the industrial revolution, technology has advanced in two directions, one toward making and moving physical things and the other toward processing information to predict the future. Over the past thirty years, however, capital has leaned heavily toward the second, and the expansion of the physical base has fallen behind. The resulting supply constraint narrows the room for large investments to be conceived at all, raises the prices of the goods and services automation never reached, such as housing, childcare, schooling, and medicine, and holds down births and demand, in what amounts to a second Malthusian trap.

This thesis therefore looks for a way to remove the constraint. To that end, it questions economic and social arrangements designed on the premise of scarcity, and proposes replacing the present system, which distributes income according to contributions of labor, with one in which every citizen holds a stake in automated productive capital from birth. People hold capital before they ever work and can give their time to creating value in the full sense rather than to productivity. Drawing on service-dominant logic, the thesis also explores treating use-value, the benefit that arises when something is used and that price and output alone cannot capture, as the measure of economic value.

On the far side of the constraint, societies regain the capacity to conceive and build on a large scale, births and demand recover, and that demand sets off a cycle of further investment and expanding supply. Symptoms such as population collapse ease without being treated one at a time.

The later sections assess nine of the world's leading clusters and compare an American techno-bloc built on a division of labor with a Chinese one built on vertical integration. They then argue for closer ties between the United States, the UAE, and Japan-Korea-Taiwan, and propose a resource integrator, an organization that connects the capital, technology, energy, sites, and permits dispersed across states and firms. Finally, they set out ten priority areas for investment and, through eleven predictions, each with the observation that would show it wrong, state the central proposition as a testable hypothesis.

detail.abstract: German debate on the recognition of foreign professional qualifications (Anerkennung ausländischer Berufsqualifikationen) is dominated by the assumption that administrative slowness is the principal obstacle, and by the corollary that private intermediaries create value by accelerating official decisions. This paper tests that assumption against official federal and Land statistics and finds it unsupported. In Baden‐Württemberg the median time to a first decision was twenty days in 2024, and the central recognition body for chamber occupations averaged sixty‐nine days from complete sub mission. The binding constraints lie elsewhere: upstream in applicant‐side dossier completeness, which alone starts the statutory clock, and downstream in the compensatory‐measure tail, where roughly forty‐five per cent of decided federal cases land and where the national average interval from order to final decision reached 490 days by 2021. A further friction is the filing channel: the authority handling approximately sixty per cent of Baden‐Württemberg procedures requires exclusively postal submission, including expiry‐dated originals valid for three months, while the chamber route accepts colour copies and electronic files. The paper then argues normatively that the Rechtsdi enstleistungsgesetz, the Zahlungsdiensteaufsichtsgesetz, the Geldwäschegesetz, the General Data Protection Regulation and the Artificial Intelligence Act jointly define a narrow compliance corridor determining which remedies a private intermediary may lawfully supply, and that this corridor — not market demand — shapes viable service design. Within it, the tractable remedy is a deterministic, versioned Policy‐as‐Code rule layer combined with statutorily permitted funding advice under § 5(2) no. 3 RDG, rather than paid legal advice or custody of official fees. Evidence was collected through an eight‐model independent‐replication design; conflicting figures are reported as conflicts rather than silently reconciled.

detail.abstract: The chapter provides a roadmap for how philosophers of science can engage more with financial economics. It argues that financial economics is best characterized by its use of models and its performative nature. This is demonstrated by focusing on the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), the centre stage model of asset pricing that enjoys enduring popularity in academic research and industry practice. Assessing the epistemic performance of financial economics, the chapter argues that the model-based and performative character of financial economics is: (1) visible in the history of its emergence and its current scientific practice, (2) central to the kind of insights it aims to generate, and (3) key to understand what kind of ethical values are at play. detail.abstract: FIRE stands for 'Financial Independence, Retire Early'. Those who adopt the FIRE lifestyle aim at achieving financial independence as early as possible in their lives. They do so by focusing on earning and saving in their younger years, so as to accumulate enough financial wealth that allows them to retire early. We argue that FIRE has what we term 'deliberative value'. FIRE is a tool that can help individuals think about the bottom-line consequences of their cares and concerns. We argue that unlocking the deliberative value of FIRE crucially depends on individuals reflecting about the value concepts that motivate their FIRE lifestyle choice. Adopted without reflection, FIRE can be dangerous. And yet, 'the examined FIRE may be worth starting', because it can be a tool for the effective pursuit of one's adopted deliberative values. To illustrate this, we provide a comprehensive survey of relevant approaches from philosophy and economics that pertain to scheduling preferences, time discounting, intertemporal rationality, life-planning, freedom, the value of work, broader notions of the good, and individualism, amongst others. We suggest that empirical work is needed to investigate the social effects of FIRE. We also suggest that philosophers invested in specific debates about value concepts would do well to integrate FIRE into the set of examples they theorize about, as it can serve as an instructive case study.

detail.abstract: Stochastic dominance is a well-established tool both for the comparison of two random variables and as a constraint in optimization problems. However, it can be unnecessarily strict. This has motivated the introduction of concepts like almost stochastic dominance and measures of stochastic non-dominance, which have been previously applied mainly to pairwise comparison between two given random variables. To allow a relaxation of stochastic dominance during the optimization process, this paper introduces tractable formulations of optimization problems where the measures of stochastic non-dominance are used in the constraints. This widens the feasible sets by allowing the variables to differ from those that dominate the benchmark by a specified level of Wasserstein distance. The relationship between such relaxation and the expected utility is also explored. The benefits of stochastic non-dominance constraints are demonstrated through an application to a portfolio selection problem using daily return data from 49 U.S. industry representative portfolios. The out-of-sample moving window analysis over 96 years shows that allowing small measures of second-degree stochastic non-dominance, especially when the Wasserstein distance of order two is considered, results in significantly higher out-of-sample returns while maintaining a similar level of risk when compared to the classical second-degree or third-degree stochastic dominance constraints.

This research analyses the dynamics of International Development Cooperation (IDC) and Official Development Assistance (ODA) in Nepal between 2010 and 2019 and unfolding the historical commencement, focusing on the bilateral and multilateral engagement of the World Bank Group (WBG) alongside major Western and non-Western donor agencies. The research evaluates the transition from concessional aid toward non-concessional market loans aimed at achieving middle-income country status after meticulously analysing official disbursement datasets, aid fragmentation, and the implementation of Nepal’s 2019 International Development Cooperation Policy within the context of federalization. David Harvey’s critical framework on neoliberalism facilitated the paper to examine the structural influence of the World Bank’s Country Partnership Strategies (CPS) and Country Partnership Frameworks (CPF) across primary social elements, particularly education, healthcare, and natural resources, where annual disbursements reached $242 million USD in FY 2018/19. The findings reveal that liberalisation policies, privatization, and decentralization principles embedded in international development frameworks have structurally distorted public service delivery, increasing market dependence while shifting accountability for systemic social sector challenges onto national administrative planning. The paper provides theoretical and empirical insights into foreign aid governance, geopolitical alignment, and international financial institution dynamics in developing economies undergoing administrative federal transition.

detail.abstract: Leverage can preserve information about a hidden volatility drift as covariance shrinks, provided its response propagates through the latent dynamics. For a bivariate Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model observed through noisy log-price levels on a fixed grid, we prove exact identification at positive covariance and adaptive squared drift risk of order min{1, [n(s² + se²)]⁻¹}, where n counts observation blocks, s is the covariance scale and e the leverage amplitude. Matching lower bounds on specified drift neighborhoods use the full price law. Dynamically exciting leverage thus permits learning where zero leverage prevents uniform consistency. Nuisance parameters are unknown; confidence coverage includes zero covariance and absent excitation. Precision requires fixed excitation and residual covariance margins, fixed positive level noise, a nonaliased drift branch and a sufficiently small, unevaluated covariance ceiling.

detail.abstract: Limited green construction adoption raises a persistent question: why do stakeholders recognise the desirability of sustainable construction yet remain reluctant to adopt it? This synthesis revisits the theoretical model developed by Hammond et al. (2021), reconceptualising its twelve hypotheses as behavioural mechanisms nested within two interconnected decision-making problems: cooperative coordination and the present-future trade-off of cost and benefits. The cooperative coordination problem concerns uncertainty about whether other stakeholders will cooperate and whether individual contributions will produce meaningful collective outcomes. The present-future trade-off of costs and benefits problem concerns the allocation of immediate resources to practices whose benefits may be delayed, uncertain or distributed among other actors. Social norms, trust in others' action, personal dilemma, loss aversion and short-term self-interest explain how stakeholders interpret and respond to these conditions. Rather than treating the hypotheses as twelve separate explanations, the synthesis organises them into coordination mechanisms, temporal incentive mechanisms and mechanisms connecting the two problems. It proposes that reluctance to adopt green construction can arise when maintaining established practices appears preferable within the prevailing decision environment. This interpretation provides a foundation for examining resistance to change as a decision-making problem and for designing interventions that address both the credibility of cooperation and the distribution of adoption costs and benefits.

detail.abstract: Six years of research moved the throughput of public Layer-1 blockchains by two orders of magnitude, and the field cannot say what any of it costs in deployment or compare one deployed system to another. From a systematization of 810 screened records we audited 299 published performance claims and built a 200-row matrix pairing each speedup mechanism with its documented cost. Of 92 numeric throughput figures, 14 carry a validator count that can be corroborated in the source text and 6 of those come from the system's own paper; 87 of the 299 claims are quotations of other papers or vendor material rather than measurements. Thirty of the 200 costs are paid at a different layer of the stack from the one that earns the benefit, 37 rest on production measurement, and the two systems with the largest deployed throughput have no archival description of their core mechanisms. We argue that throughput figures have ceased to function as scientific results, that the cause is evaluating mechanisms in isolation when they are deployed as stacks, and that the remedy is procedural. We propose a seven-field Performance Claim Card, an attribution rule for comparison tables, evidence grading as a reporting norm, and a distinction between mechanism evaluation and stack evaluation that venues can enforce through artifact review.

detail.abstract: Standard analyses of retirement adequacy focus on financial metrics such as contribution rates and replacement ratios, while climate scenario studies typically emphasize broad macroeconomic outcomes. Neither approach, however, directly addresses what matters most to individuals: the quality of life in retirement. Retirement security under climate change is inherently multidimensional, shaped not only by financial wealth but also by health systems, infrastructure, environmental conditions, and social resilience. We develop an integrated framework that combines qualitative climate scenario narratives with quantitative macro-financial modelling to assess retirement outcomes in the United Kingdom through 2050. We construct three internally consistent SSP-RCP-based scenarios and translate them into indicators of retirees' lived experience alongside climate-damage-adjusted macroeconomic trajectories, which inform long-term asset return assumptions and retirement income projections. The results show that financial adequacy metrics alone can misrepresent retirement resilience. Relatively small differences in expected investment returns can coexist with large divergences in longevity, health, service reliability, and everyday living conditions. By linking narratives with numbers, the framework clarifies how socioeconomic environments and financial outcomes interact, providing a more decision-relevant assessment of climate-related retirement risks for pension funds, long-horizon investors, and policymakers.

detail.abstract:
Beginning in the early 2000s, China’s housing sector expanded at an extraordinary pace.
By 2016 housing-related activities accounted for nearly 29% of GDP. A distinctive feature of
this expansion is a persistent wedge between completed construction and market absorption.
To capture this phenomenon, this paper develops a two-sector dynamic stochastic general
equilibrium (DSGE) model in which newly completed units are sold through a frictional re-
tail housing market, so that a stock of completed-but-unsold housing emerges endogenously
as a cyclical state variable. The model is estimated with Bayesian methods using Chinese
quarterly data for the period 2004Q4–2023Q4. The estimated model reproduces the high
relative volatilities of housing prices, construction, and new house purchases. The model also
captures the comovement between the housing market variables and the aggregate economy
observed in the data. Our variance decomposition shows that housing productivity shocks
are the primary driver of fluctuations in housing construction, whereas shocks to buyer search
attempts dominate fluctuations in housing prices, market tightness, and model-implied in-

detail.abstract: Security is not merely a condition of social order; it is an essential foundation for productive economic activity and sustainable development. Businesses require a predictable environment in which workers can travel safely, goods can move through markets, assets can be protected, contracts can be enforced and investment decisions can be made with reasonable confidence. Where these conditions deteriorate, insecurity begins to operate as an economic constraint rather than only a security or criminal justice problem. This article examines the relationship between insecurity, kidnapping, governance deficits, corruption and business development in Nigeria. It argues that persistent insecurity affects the economy through several interconnected channels, including higher transaction and security costs, disrupted transportation and supply chains, reduced investment, restricted labour mobility, weaker human capital formation, lower productivity and increased uncertainty. These effects are particularly significant because insecurity changes economic behaviour before a violent incident necessarily occurs. Travellers alter routes, transport operators increase prices, workers become reluctant to accept assignments in high risk areas, farmers reduce access to distant farms and businesses allocate resources to security measures that would otherwise support productive expansion. The article also examines the evolution of kidnapping from high-profile school abductions, including the 2014 Chibok abduction, to incidents affecting students, teachers, schoolchildren, workers, prospective National Youth Service Corps members and ordinary travellers. The experience of insecurity on routes such as the Kaduna–Abuja highway and incidents affecting travellers in Kogi demonstrate how insecurity can transform essential transport infrastructure into an economic risk. The Chibok experience further illustrates that the cost of insecurity extends beyond immediate physical harm: when children cannot safely attend school, a society risks losing part of its future human capital. Drawing on institutional economics, transaction cost economics, human capital theory and investment climate perspectives, the article develops an integrated framework linking insecurity to business performance and sustainable development. Evidence from Ede and Okafor (2023), using Nigerian firm level data and kidnapping indicators, further supports a negative relationship between kidnapping and foreign ownership. The article concludes that Nigeria's security crisis cannot be addressed through military or policing responses alone. Sustainable development requires simultaneous improvements in security, governance, accountability, infrastructure, justice, human capital development and private sector resilience. Security is both influenced by broader development conditions and an important enabling condition for sustained development.

(c) Conversely, above-median earners exhibit similar behavior across countries. detail.abstract: Human rights treaties are routinely described as limits on sovereignty, and sovereignty as the principal obstacle to global human rights protection. detail.abstract: In CRSP's legacy flat-file format, a day on which a security did not trade carried a bid/ask-midpoint price with a negative sign, and screening on prc < 0 removed such days. A single such holding raises a strategy's annualised Sharpe ratio to 1.97. The remedy is to screen on DlyPrcFlg instead.

detail.abstract: Genocide occupies the symbolic apex of international criminal law, yet the decentralised enforcement of that law through universal jurisdiction has to operate on the evidence and procedural gateways that national courts actually possess. This article asks under what conditions the choice among genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity as charging categories, together with the jurisdictional design of the forum state, determines whether universal jurisdiction yields accountability for conduct that harms civilians. Using doctrinal analysis of the Genocide Convention, the Geneva Conventions and the Rome Statute, jurisprudential analysis of decisions of the International Court of Justice, the ad hoc tribunals and national courts, and a purposive comparison of Germany, France, Belgium, Spain, Argentina and the Senegalese-African Union arrangement for Hissène Habré, the article develops a two-channel account. In the individual-prosecution channel before national courts, the specific-intent requirement of genocide, and the political demand for the genocide label, make it an unreliable organising category. The article defends conduct-first charging, in which investigators build cases around the widest provable evidentiary base and add genocide where intent evidence supports it, combined with presence-anchored, subsidiarity-conditioned jurisdiction. The argument is doctrinal and normative rather than empirical, the comparison is illustrative rather than statistical, and the article identifies the evidence that would falsify or narrow its thesis. The contribution is an analytical distinction and an interpretive standard for prosecutors and legislators, not a new regime.

detail.abstract: Nigeria has produced development plans for eight decades, from the colonial Ten-Year Plan of 1946 to the National Development Plan 2021-2025 and Agenda 2050. detail.abstract: This paper develops a vector-autoregressive framework for time series whose primitive observations are random compact convex sets. detail.abstract: How does audience identity shape public behavior when people favor their own social groups and expect others to do the same? detail.abstract: This paper examines how differences in discretion embedded in U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) and the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) generate book-tax differences (BTD). detail.abstract: Food insufficiency has long disproportionately affected marginalized communities, including American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN) populations, and the economic disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic both expanded food insufficiency measurement and led to a surge in related research. detail.abstract: Performance-linked finance may suit small enterprises whose earnings and cash receipts vary, but making such finance operational requires more than agreeing on a percentage share of business performance. The central challenge is to define how the investor's entitlement will be calculated, how payment difficulties will be handled, and how the investment will ultimately be settled-while preserving meaningful risk sharing and keeping delivery costs manageable. This paper examines that challenge through practitioner-led action research involving twelve semi-formal enterprises in India, using contracts, operating records, reconciled investor receipts and retrospective accounts. Under the contract implemented in the pilot, the investor's entitlement was linked to reported monthly surplus, and the investor's profit-sharing percentage declined as capital was returned. A loss month created no new entitlement, but the loss was not carried forward to reduce entitlement in later profitable months. Reported surplus also did not necessarily mean that the enterprise had sufficient cash to make the corresponding payment. Reconciliation of receipts establishes what the investor received, but does not reconstruct every historical entitlement or due date. Similarly, gaps in information and expectations that were never formally agreed do not, by themselves, establish misconduct. Payment variability, temporary accommodation of payment difficulties and the investor's absorption of terminal business loss are therefore distinct dimensions of risk sharing and should be assessed separately. Drawing on these operating problems, the paper proposes rules for selection and additional investment, separate classifications for payment and information states, and a common record linking evidence, decisions, receipts and recovery actions. These are proposals for testing; the pilot did not validate selection for productive growth or demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed operating rules. Evaluation must therefore distinguish investor outcomes, delivery costs, manager viability and value to the entrepreneur, including reporting burden and payment stress. Because the twelve enterprises were not randomly selected, the practitioner was directly involved, observations were uneven and there was no comparison group, the study cannot support causal impact claims or conclusions about sustainable returns at scale. detail.abstract:
Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence while its direction is still deeply uncertain. AI might remain a powerful tool that people gradually allow to act on its own, or it might develop into a population of agents with interests of its own. This report sets AI aside and follows two imaginary technologies with similar economics: an augmentation pill that people increasingly let act for them, and a lab-grown "DishBrain" that may someday have interests of its own. Each is traced through a series of stages. At every stage the report asks which policies would help, and whether those policies would still work at later stages. The results are then mapped back to AI.

Both pathways cross a visibility threshold: a point past which the causes of a system's behavior can no longer be established from outside. Two familiar tools fail at that threshold. One is labeling machine-made work. The other is assigning blame to whoever caused a harm. The report proposes eighteen policies. Eleven of them hold on both pathways because they attach to things that stay observable: physical inputs, named responsible parties, measurable effects, and the system as a whole. Each policy is tested for durability past the threshold, and also for its cost, who bears that cost, and its potential for abuse. A reserved class of state decisions keeps a right to a human decision-maker that never sunsets.

detail.abstract: Regulators often condition policy on economic headroom, the distance between a consequential boundary and an institution's current position. When these conditions fail, the best headroom-only correction is a weighted projection of the wedge, and its residual prices a further instrument. The span and projection results are special cases of the general theory of second-best corrective regulation; the fiber and integrability conditions, and the fact that the reporting rule chooses the constraint, are specific to headroom. An example shows that integrability can fail, so that no headroom schedule implements the planner's rule, although span holds at every allocation and no two types report the same headroom. detail.abstract: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's 2022 election renewed expectations of Brazilian environmental leadership, particularly in Amazon conservation. This study examines whether durable domestic institutional capacity supports this renewed international leadership. Drawing on official reports, satellite data, federal budget execution records (2005-2026), and the 2022 campaign platform, we combine environmental and political-institutional analyses to examine four dimensions of the 2022-2026 period: (i) fire activity as a high-frequency indicator of forest pressure; (ii) infrastructure development and hydrocarbon licensing, including the BR-319 highway and oil exploration along the Equatorial Margin; (iii) demand for critical minerals associated with artificial intelligence and its intersection with illegal mining in Indigenous territories; and (iv) the fiscal architecture of environmental enforcement. Deforestation declined substantially after 2022, but fire hotspots reached their highest level since 2007 in 2024, amid severe droughts. The Ministry of the Environment's headline budget rose from R$3.5 billion in 2022 to R$47.9 billion in 2026, driven almost entirely by the National Fund on Climate Change. Enforcement funding, however, remained volatile and dependent on midyear emergency credits, continuing a pattern observed under previous administrations. The 2026 general election, in which the opposition candidate led the first round while advocating faster environmental licensing and fiscal consolidation, further exposes the vulnerability of environmental policy to electoral change. Brazil's international environmental leadership thus remains constrained by an enforcement apparatus reliant on unstable funding and emergency allocations across successive administrations. Amazon protection requires sustained state commitment and stable, legally protected enforcement funding that does not depend on the government in office.

detail.abstract: Does assignment to a web-first survey sequence change how respondents report socially sensitive attitudes and behaviors? Using randomized mode-sequence assignment in the 2022 and 2024 General Social Survey (GSS), this study separates four features that are often conflated in mixed-mode research: randomized sequence assignment, survey response, final completed mode, and population weighting. Crossover is substantial: pooled across waves, 62.7 percent of Web-first assignees complete on the web, compared with 33.2 percent of face-to-face-first assignees. The intent-to-treat estimates therefore capture the effect of assignment to a fieldwork sequence rather than a pure web-versus-face-to-face mode contrast. Across a pooled index of socially sensitive reporting, there is little evidence of a large uniform shift. An unweighted comparison among observed completers shows a small positive effect on civic reporting, driven mainly by self-reported voting, but the pattern is absent under the GSS-recommended nonresponse-adjusted post-stratification weight (WTSSNRPS) and under the alternative post-stratification weight (WTSSPS). Randomization inference leads to the same qualitative conclusion. The analysis shows why as-treated comparisons of completed mode can be misleading in sequential mixed-mode designs and why weighted and unweighted estimates may target different populations. Overall, Web-first assignment does not produce a robust broad change in socially sensitive reporting, although modest domain-specific effects remain possible.

detail.abstract: From March 2020 to November 2021 the United States restricted non-essential travel across its land borders with Canada and Mexico. Inbound person crossings at U.S.-Canada land ports fell to 3 percent of their 2019 level, recovered only slowly, and regained their 2019 level in 2024 before falling again to 57 percent by March 2026; crossings at U.S.-Mexico ports fell by roughly 70 percent at the trough and had largely recovered by late 2021. I combine port-level crossing data with a county-by-sector panel from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages for 2015-2026 to estimate how the loss of cross-border visitors affected employment in nearby U.S. counties. Each port's traffic is allocated to surrounding counties with a gravity rule, which yields a county-level measure of exposure and a time-varying visitor shortfall. Without allowing for pre-existing trends, the average restriction-period shortfall of 88 percent is associated with a 2.3 log point decline in retail employment in Canada-port counties (95 percent randomization confidence interval -4.3 to -0.4). Retail employment in these counties was already declining relative to comparison counties before 2020, however, and once treated-group linear trends are removed the estimate falls to -0.75 log points (-4.0 to +2.1). Accommodation and food services show no effect during the restrictions, and manufacturing, used as a placebo, shows none. Estimates for Mexico-port counties are larger but imprecise. Across specifications, the data rule out retail employment losses larger than about four log points in Canada-port counties. I discuss why the employment response may be muted: the restrictions also kept border residents' spending at home, and employment is a coarser margin than sales.

detail.abstract: Mining provides essential raw materials but is an increasingly important driver of biodiversity loss. Global mining assessments have mapped mining-driven ecosystem degradation at unprecedented resolution, but linking these impacts to the companies driving them remains challenging. Here, we develop a tractable framework that combines satellite-derived mining land use, geolocated asset-level data, and ecological data to trace mining in protected areas and mining-driven species extinction risks from individual mines to their corporate owners, and estimate the biodiversity footprints of thousands of mining companies worldwide. Mining threats to biodiversity concentrate in the Global South and Australia, with a substantial share driven by North American, Western European, and East Asian corporations, whose overseas biodiversity footprints often exceed those of their home countries' mining sectors by orders of magnitude. In Latin America and Sub-Saharan Africa, these threats concentrate in countries with weak resource governance, compounding the risk of irreversible natural capital loss with little contribution to local development. Extinction risks are highly concentrated within the mining sector, as certain companies hold projects in some of the most biodiversity-rich and threatened regions on Earth. Comparing our footprint estimates with disclosure-based indicators suggests widespread underreporting of these impacts in the mining sector. Our study demonstrates that coupling global mining assessments with asset-level data can greatly reduce these information asymmetries and enhance corporate accountability.

detail.abstract: Electricity markets are characterized by nonlinear supply and demand schedules, so a global energy crisis may change not only price levels but also the transmission of supply and demand shocks. Using high-frequency data from the Japanese wholesale electricity market, we examine this mechanism with two complementary approaches. First, we estimate impulse responses using local projections with external instruments before and during the global energy crisis, excluding a Japan-specific price spike in the winter of 2020–2021. During the crisis, the impact response of prices to demand shocks becomes larger, whereas the response to supply shocks is smaller on impact and builds gradually over several weeks. These patterns are consistent with an upward shift in the kinked supply curve that moved the equilibrium into a steeper segment of supply and a flatter, high-price segment of demand. Second, a historical decomposition based on a sign-identified structural vector autoregression indicates that the persistent elevation of prices during the crisis was associated mainly with supply-side forces, while demand-side forces partially offset the increase. Taken together, the results suggest that the global energy crisis altered both price levels and the mechanism through which supply and demand shocks were transmitted to prices.

detail.abstract: The sharp rise in European wholesale electricity prices during the recent energy crisis renewed debate over whether faster renewable deployment can lower and stabilise consumer costs, a premise underlying the revised renewable energy targets of the European Union. This study examines whether renewable electricity generation reduces wholesale prices across a panel of European countries observed over the past decade. The empirical strategy addresses two identification concerns dynamic panel methods do not handle well here: price persistence from year to year and cross-sectional dependence from shared fuel markets and cross-border interconnection. Short-T, factor-robust dynamic panel estimators are applied, including a diagnostic estimator that combines cross-sectional averaging with generalised method of moments instrumentation to test the compatibility of the two corrections directly. Renewable generation and wind in particular is associated with lower wholesale prices, consistently across estimators that differ in how they address cross-sectional dependence. Solar shows a less consistent relationship with price and the price-suppressing effect of renewables varies across European regions and strengthens under higher economic uncertainty. The findings survive a check for reverse causality and are not sensitive to the assumed number of common factors. These results speak to ongoing European policy debates over the pace of renewable deployment and its effect on consumer electricity costs.

detail.abstract: We develop a structural, dual-dimensional view of tail risk and show how to extract the return-relevant component from existing proxies. In a model with heterogeneous beliefs, observed tail-risk measures are noisy mixtures of ex-ante disaster concerns and ex-post realizations with underreaction. Guided by this framework, we use partial least squares (PLS) to construct an aggregate tail-risk index, TRPLS  , from 18 U.S. option-, return-, and macro-based proxies.  TRPLS  strongly and positively predicts the U.S. equity premium in- and out-of-sample, outperforms leading macro and uncertainty predictors, and delivers sizable gains in a mean–variance asset-allocation exercise. Decompositions show that TRPLS  loads on both ex-ante and ex-post channels, has stronger predictive power in low-sentiment and high-uncertainty states, and forecasts primarily cash-flow news rather than discount-rate news.

detail.abstract: Liquidity is not merely a property of an institution’s balance sheet; it is a market-wide outcomeshaped by what everyone else is doing. detail.abstract: The security of critical mineral supplies, including cobalt, has become a central concern for China's energy transition and carbon reduction goals. This study couples a Bayesian network–Monte Carlo (BN-MC) model with a computable general equilibrium model to quantify the long-term dynamic effects of uncertainty in cobalt supply chain risks on the economy, CO₂ emissions, and the energy mix. Three findings emerge. First, although refined cobalt accounts for less than 0.01% of China's GDP, its critical role in the electric vehicle supply chain means that supply disruptions have macroeconomic effects far larger than the sector's size would suggest. In the extreme risk scenario (R = 80%), China's real GDP in 2027 is 0.29% below the business-as-usual (BAU) level. Relative to the nationally determined contribution (NDC) scenario, cobalt supply chain risks cause an additional GDP loss of approximately US$61.4 billion. Second, the small aggregate effect on CO₂ emissions should not obscure an underlying economic contraction. Slower electric vehicle adoption raises transport emissions, while the economic downturn and the contraction of electricity-intensive manufacturing reduce coal-fired power use. These effects offset each other, leaving aggregate emissions unable to capture the loss of mitigation benefits caused by the disruption. Third, over the long term, cobalt supply chain risks redirect capital from electric vehicles and batteries toward low-carbon technologies, including wind, solar photovoltaics, nuclear power, and carbon capture and storage (CCS), accelerating the energy transition. These results reveal how critical mineral constraints reshape emissions reduction pathways and provide quantitative evidence to inform the development of early warning systems and responses to supply chain uncertainty.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether finer price granularity improves allocative efficiency by revealing spatial scarcity that was previously hidden under a single administrative price. Electricity markets are a suitable context: transmission constraints are physical, while zone boundaries are an administrative choice, so the same constraint can be priced explicitly or resolved implicitly depending on where the boundary is drawn. We study the Norwegian market reform of 13 April 2009, through which the NO2 zone was divided into an importing area (the redefined NO2) and an exporting area (NO3), using hourly data over a ±100-day window. By applying a difference-in-differences analysis, we identify a significant price increase of +0.922 €/MWh in NO2 compared to the unaffected control zone NO1, corroborated by a pair-difference analysis and an event study that shows no pre-existing trends. The contrasting behaviour of the two interfaces around the new zone highlights that the reform priced a pre-existing constraint rather than creating a new one. The implied efficiency gain is small, about €315,000 per year on an annualised basis, but the transfer from consumers to producers is about 120 times larger. On its own, a static efficiency gain does not justify splitting a zone with a moderate internal constraint. The case for reconfiguration rests mainly on dynamic effects and the costs of market fragmentation.

detail.abstract: Abstract. This paper does not falsify the labor theory of value. It proves something prior: that "labor creates value," read as a proposition about a value-substance and its independent measure, never acquired the measurement credentials such a proposition requires. Every piece of evidence is drawn from concessions already signed by the tradition that defends or repairs the claim: Marx's own textual apparatus of "socially necessary" labor time and the reduction of complex to simple labor; the collective record of a century of transformation-problem literature; and the constitution thesis of the value-form school. Together these concessions establish that heterogeneous labor can enter a value system only by way of a mechanism that first renders it commensurable (constitutivity); and that from the necessity of commensuration, the necessity of labor as its content does not follow (non-necessity) — the opponent's central derivation, the distillation argument, fails on the selectivity of its abstraction. "Labor creates value" is therefore at most a candidate rule of commensuration; and as a candidate rule it cannot win back ontological standing in either of its two possible fates, adopted or not adopted (dominance). The verdict is then settled along the chain of dependency: every conclusion whose proof cannot dispense with the labor measure of value — surplus value, the rate of exploitation — inherits the measure's conventional status; and the empirical success of the theory as a whole cannot flow back to recharge its base, because confirmation, traced class by class to its target, never lands on "labor is the necessary content of commensuration." The paper closes by listing the six ways it can be defeated.

detail.abstract: AI agents increasingly operate through tools, memory, delegated authority, external information, persistent state, and multi-agent coordination. Penetration testing that focuses on one model endpoint or terminal action can therefore miss weaknesses that emerge across the wider agentic process. This paper proposes an evidence-governed model for penetration testing of agents, agentic processes, and agent organizations. Controlled adversarial pressure is treated as a method of security-evidence acquisition whose findings remain bounded by the tested configuration, state, visibility, and execution conditions. The model binds the governed test to the state in which it was executed and to the evidence that supports its claims. Because testing can itself alter persistent or adaptive state, test-exposed instances are treated as experimental artifacts rather than automatically reusable production artifacts. The paper separates test-induced adaptation from validated hardening and uses a clean-baseline retest loop for bounded mitigation claims. It then applies the model to recurring problems of trust, authority, persistent state, external assessment, and agentic security controls. The contribution is conceptual and does not introduce a new exploit technique, autonomous attack system, or empirical benchmark.

detail.abstract:
Risk reports describe distances to declared boundaries but do not necessarily describe the actions available to repair them. This paper applies established Pareto criticality and convex separation to an attainable headroom-change cone formed from risk sensitivities and feasible directions. A pair is in conflict when no feasible direction strictly improves both margins; separating weights price their tradeoff. Under explicit instrument restrictions, costly protection creates conflict exactly when the funding resource cannot be replenished without surrendering protection. After normalizing margin units, the paper bounds bottleneck switching and characterizes an affine protocol in which independently assigned protective routes amplify damage. A stylized Basel III balance sheet computes the conflict thresholds and shows that extending the funding menu can change supporting prices even when conflict classifications are unchanged. A solved repair problem illustrates how resource availability changes feasibility despite identical margin levels. Chinese mutual-fund evidence is presented as observational diagnostics, not a causal test of the cone: contractual equity-floor room is measured on its documented denominator, but actual drawdown limits and feasible trade sets are unobserved. The primary corrected stress-slope contrast does not show less equity-share reduction near the floor, and holdings-beta adjustments do not show a stronger near-floor response. A new same-unit typical-move comparison and a corrected conditional held-out model comparison are reported transparently as post hoc. These findings neither establish that a floor blocks trading nor validate the proposed shortfall-liquidity cycle. The contribution is an operational application of standard geometry, accompanied by a worked decision problem and evidence delineating what the available data cannot identify.

detail.abstract: Foreign exchange risk management is usually viewed as a decision that stabilizes the hedging firm's own cash flows. This paper shows that, with financial frictions and production networks, a firm's hedging also stabilizes its suppliers and customers. In a model of hedging in a production network, firms finance production before collecting revenue at a borrowing rate that falls with their financial position. By shifting resources across exchange-rate states, hedging changes a firm's borrowing costs, prices, and input purchases, and thereby the costs and demand of connected firms. Using new hand-collected data on U.S. firms' foreign exchange derivatives from 10-K filings, linked to their supply-chain relationships, I find that when a firm's customers (suppliers) first begin to hedge, the volatility of its sales (cost of goods sold) falls by 3.1 percentage points relative to matched firms. In a model calibrated to the U.S. input-output network, hedging offsets one-quarter to two-fifths of the volatility amplification generated by the borrowing-cost channel. An industry's own hedge accounts for almost all of the stabilization of its net worth, whereas the hedging of other industries accounts for about half of the stabilization of its output, and hedging affects other industries most when undertaken by central suppliers. Foreign exchange risk management is thus both a private stabilizer of financial positions and a network stabilizer of real activity.

detail.abstract: Metal-phenolic networks (MPNs), formed by coordination between polyphenols and metal ions, have been assembled almost entirely in water. This excludes substrates that dissolve or degrade in aqueous media, among them urea and other fertilizer salts, many crystalline actives, and watersoluble polymers. Nonaqueous assembly has recently been introduced to remove this restriction, and a solvent-free mechanochemical route has followed. This review synthesizes the literature on MPN assembly, the principles by which solvents govern metal-ligand coordination, and the small body of work that applies these ideas to soluble substrates. We examine what is established, namely that iron-tannic acid coatings of micrometre thickness can be formed on urea in an organic solvent and that solid-state urea-MPN matrices can be produced mechanochemically, and what remains hypothetical. Gaps are identified in mechanistic understanding, solvent selection, thickness control, characterization, and environmental assessment. We propose a four-stage conceptual framework linking solvent choice, substrate-triggered complexation, deposition, and downstream performance, expressed as testable hypotheses rather than results. Applications in controlled-release fertilizers are the best documented, while extensions to other soluble materials are discussed as prospects. We conclude with priorities for independent replication, standardized reporting, and green-solvent evaluation. Throughout, the review separates findings reported in the literature from interpretation and from proposed future work.

detail.abstract:
Blockchain technology has emerged as a transformative innovation, introducing new approaches to decentralization, transparency, and trust. Since the introduction of Bitcoin in 2008, its applications have expanded beyond cryptocurrencies, creating significant opportunities and challenges for existing legal systems.

This dissertation examines the adequacy of current legal and regulatory frameworks governing blockchain technology through a comparative analysis of nine selected jurisdictions. It explores how different regulatory approaches address cryptocurrencies, digital assets, and emerging applications such as Decentralized Finance (DeFi) and Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs).

Using doctrinal and comparative legal methodologies, the research identifies regulatory gaps, inconsistencies, and challenges arising from the decentralized nature of blockchain technology. Particular attention is given to balancing innovation with legal certainty, investor protection, and regulatory compliance.

The dissertation evaluates the limitations of existing legal frameworks and proposes policy recommendations for more flexible, coherent, and technology-responsive regulation. Ultimately, it aims to contribute to the development of legal systems capable of supporting blockchain innovation while addressing associated risks and facilitating the transition toward an increasingly decentralized digital environment.

detail.abstract: The way research is produced has changed. Generative AI can now assist with literature search, synthesis, coding, and drafting at a speed and scale that was not previously possible. Yet research evaluation still relies on citation counts, journal prestige, and publication volume-metrics that measure attention, not novelty. As AI makes it easier to produce stylistically sophisticated work that recombines existing ideas, the gap between what these metrics capture and what actually constitutes intellectual contribution is widening. This paper introduces the AI-Powered Novelty Index, a new metric that measures academic novelty directly from a paper's content. The index uses LLM embeddings to compute how far a paper's core claims deviate from the semantic space of existing academic work. The technical pipeline uses OpenAlex, FAISS-based nearest-neighbour retrieval, and cosine distance, and is designed for scalability, transparency, and reproducibility. The paper also proposes a hypothesis: that Citation Herding and the Snowball Effect shape which papers are recognised as novel, and that the Sleeping Beauty coefficient provides one validation parameter for detecting it. The paper argues that measuring novelty directly-rather than through proxies-is both possible and necessary in an era of AI-accelerated research production.

detail.abstract: Artificial-intelligence deployment in radiology is commonly modeled using a small set of pure architectures: sequential triage, mechanical OR adjudication, mechanical AND adjudication, and strict human-final-arbiter review. These rules are analytically convenient but may not describe AI-visible workflows in which the radiologist retains final authority and responds selectively to discordant AI outputs. This paper develops a unified selective-adjudication framework for AI-human reading. Two response parameters govern the treatment of disagreement: one determines how often an AI-positive, human-negative classification becomes finally positive, and the other determines how often an AI-negative, human-positive classification becomes finally negative. The resulting model nests strict human-final-arbiter, mechanical OR, mechanical AND, and AI-final-arbiter adjudication as limiting cases. Closed-form expressions connect standalone AI and human operating characteristics to system-level sensitivity and specificity under conditional independence, while a joint-probability formulation permits dependence to be retained when paired data are available. The diagnostic framework is then incorporated into an expected-cost model and compared with human-only interpretation and sequential AI triage. The analysis shows that diagnostic equivalence does not imply economic equivalence: workflows that produce the same final classifications may differ materially because sequential triage conditions human interpretation on the AI result, whereas concurrent adjudication requires both readings. The framework clarifies how deployment architecture, disagreement resolution, disease prevalence, diagnostic error costs, and interpretation costs jointly determine the clinical and economic consequences of AI-assisted reading.

detail.abstract:
In modern AI workflows where prediction and decision-making are separated, an upstream prediction team must serve unknown or heterogeneous downstream decision makers. Calibration, a property of predictive models, enables this separation. It requires reported probabilities to be conditionally unbiased, so they can be trusted and directly used by any downstream decision maker without task-specific correction. 

We propose Calibration Decision Loss (CDL) as a decision-theoretic calibration error. CDL is defined as the largest improvement in expected payoff obtainable by recalibrating a predictor across all bounded decision problems. By definition, CDL captures the worst-case decision loss from miscalibration and therefore directly measures whether a predictive model is trustworthy for heterogeneous downstream users. 

Our results highlight a fundamental difference between decision-theoretic error and known calibration errors. CDL counts only biases that can change decisions, whereas standard metrics such as Expected Calibration Error (ECE) average over all prediction biases, regardless of their impact on decisions. In an online setting, this perspective leads to a prediction algorithm with near-optimal expected CDL, improving upon decision-making guarantees obtained by optimizing canonical calibration errors.
